lawyer:
M. H. Khandker, Senior Advocate, with B.B. Roy Chowdhury and B.K. Das, Advocates, instructed by S.M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant.
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Advocate, with Md. Shafiqur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by A. Rab-II, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent.
parties:
Salamat Khan ........ Appellant.
Vs.
Q.G. Ahad ...…. Respondent.
full_judgment:
Facts giving rise to this appeal briefly put are, that R.S. Plot No.573 of mouza Muradnagar belongs to Mr. Q.G. Ahad and R.S. Plot No.579 of the same mouza belongs to Mr. Salamat Khan the appellant. Over the demarcation of a common boundary dispute arose between the parties and Mr. Ahad, the Respondent approached the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong for demarcation of that boundary and Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1967-68 was staged and a surveyor appointed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner who surveyed the two plot and submitted a report. The appellant disagreeing with the report filed a petition in the demarcation case on 19-9-67 praying for appointment of five persons named by him including Mr. Zainul Abedin Chowdhury, Administrative Officer, Divisional Commissioner's Office, Chittagong and Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury, Member of the Provincial Assembly for deciding the dispute, and an undertaking was given that he would also abide by the decision given by any one of these five persons as arbitrator. The Respondent through his attorney A. Kusuf filed an application on 25-9-67 and agreed to the arbitration by Messers Alimullah Chowdhury and Z.A. Chowdhury. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, by an order of 28-9-67 appointed Mr. Zainul Abedin Chowdhury as the Arbitrator and Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury M.P.A. as the umpire to arbitrate the dispute according to the terms and conditions laid down therein and directed that the arbitrator should prepare a written award along with a sketch map delineating plots 573 and 579 according to demarcation and possession. In the event of a party disagreeing with the award, of the Arbitrator, the matter was to be referred, to the umpire, Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury. Both the parties on 28-9-67 executed an agreement for reference to Arbitration in accordance with the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner. The appellant, however, filed an application in the said Miscellaneous case on 7-10-67 praying for appointment of Mr. Sarafatullah M.P.A., one of the five persons named in the earlier application dated 19-9-67, in place of Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury as an umpire. The Respondent filed an objection against this petition dated 7-10-67 on 27-11-67 contending that the appointment of umpire was not called for in view of the appointment of Mr. Zainul Abedin Chowdhury as the sole Arbitrator and praying for cancellation of the appointment of umpire. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong passed on order on 27-11-67 accepting the contention of the Respondent and modifying his earlier order dated 28-9-67 to the extent that the dispute shall be referred to the sole Arbitrator, and the award so given would be binding upon both the parties. If does not appear that the order was made in presence of the Appellant. Mr. Zainul Abedin Chowdhury, the sole Arbitrator issued notice of reference on 1-11-67. After having it surveyed by a surveyor, demarcating the two plots and preparing a sketch map showing demarcation of the boundary between those plots, he on 13-2-68 made an award, the sketch map forming part thereof. This award was submitted on 3-4-68 to the Additional Deputy Commissioner, who on consultation with the local Government Pleader, returned the award to Mr. Z. A. Chowdhury asking him to take action according to law. The award was then filed in Court on 10-9-68 by the Arbitrator, Mr. Z. A. Chowdhury. 

 2. In Court the Appellant, as the opposite party filed on 27-12-68, a written objection challenging the Validity of the award of the Arbitrator both on point of law and on merit. He, however, failed to file objection within-thirty days as required by Article 158 of the Limitation Act and the Subordinate Judge by his order dated 28-12-68 held the written objection time barred. The Appellant acquiesced to this order but challenged the award on the ground that alteration of the arbitration agreement by cancelling the stipulation of umpire totally changed the agreement and made the agreement null and void. The Appellant did not consent to the alteration brought about on 27-11-67. His further objection was that the award was made beyond time and that it was unregistered. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties set aside the award and superseded the arbitration agreement. He held that the award was on 13-2-68 and the Arbitrator issued notices on 1-11-67 and so the award was made within four months from that date and was not time barred. He found flying of stamp on the award not a prerequisite for the validity of the award, and so fixing of the stamp on 9-9-68 did not make the award illegal. He next hold that want of registration did not make the award invalid. He however held that the stipulation in the arbitration agreement relating to umpire was altered by Additional Deputy Commissioner by his order dated 27-14-67 without the consent of the Appellant, who, according to him, had originally agreed to a reference to arbitration by one arbitrator arid in case of disagreement by an umpire, and so the alteration rendered the reference null and void. An appeal was preferred by the Respondent to the High Court and it was disposed of by a Division Bench. The learned Judges of the High Court Division on hearing the-parties took a different view, on the validity of the award and held that the parties agreed to have the dispute settled by an Arbitration proceeding and it was the intention of both the parties. It was found, that the agreement could be inferred from several documents and that it was not necessary that it was to be sighed. They also held that the steps taken by the appellant before Mr. Z. Abedin Chowdhury, the Arbitrator could be well understood to have been taken and done by him conscious of the order of 27-11-67. From the conduct of the parties, it was abundantly clear they gave a go-bye to a contract which provided for accepting second arbitration in case, of disagreement, and agreed to be bound by new agreement in the matter as on 27-11-67 by the sole Arbitrator. They held that it was sufficient, if a party accepted and acted on the agreement. They found that there was nothing on record to show that the Appellant raised any objection to the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner dated 27-11-67. On the contrary, he had participated in the proceeding before the sole arbitrator. They, therefore, reversed the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge and allowed the appeal without any order at to costs, set aside the order of the Subordinate Judge and made the award submitted by the sole Arbitrator, Mr. Z. Abedin Chowdhury a rule of the Court. 

 6. On an analysis of section 2(a) of the Act, we find that the requirements of law, giving authority to an arbitrator to give an award, depends upon the authority conferred by the parties by an agreement to refer their differences to arbitration. The arbitration agreement is to be a written agreement to submit present or future differences to arbitration to an arbitrator who may or may not be named. A writing incorporating an agreement to submit their differences between the contracting parties to an arbitrator is the legal mandate. If a valid arbitration agreement is there, then there need not be a formal agreement executed by the parties, nor is it required of the parties to sign. The agreement must be in writing and accepted by the parties. No particular form is necessary, it may be inferred from a set or series of documents. The view we have expressed has been taken by the Indian Supreme Court in the cases of Jugal Kishore Vs. Golbai, AIR 1955 (SC) 812; and Union of India Vs. Rallia Ram, AIR 1963 (CS) 1685. 

 9. The House of Lords in the Brogden Vs. Metropolitan Railway Company, 1877(2) Appeal Cases 666 has observed that circumstances in the conduct of two parties may establish a binding contract between them, although the agreement, reduced into writing as a draft, has not been formally executed by either. The facts are that Brogden had for some years supplied the Metropolitan Railway Company with coal. At last it was suggested by Brogden that a contract should be entered into between them. After their agents had met together the terms of agreement were drawn up by the agent of the Metropolitan Railway Company and sent to Brogden. Brogden filled up certain parts of it, which had been left in blank, and introduced the name of the gentleman who was to act as arbitrator in case of differences between the parties, wrote "approved" at the end of the paper, and signed his own name. Brogden's agent sent back the paper to the agent of the Metropolitan Railway Company, who put it in his desk, and nothing further was done in the way of a formal execution of it. Both parties for some time acted in accordance with the arrangements mentioned in the papers, coals were supplied and payments made as therein stated, and when some complaints of inexactness in the supply of coal according to the terms stated in the paper, were made by the Metropolitan Railway Company, there were explanations and excuses given by Brogden, and the "contract" was mentioned in the correspondence, and matters went on as before. Finally disagreements arose, and Brogden denied that there was any contract which bound him in the matter and it went up to the House of Lords and the noble Lords, held, that these facts, and the actual conduct of the parties, established the existence of such a contract, and there having been a clear breach of it, Brogden must be held liable upon if. It was further observed that a mere mental assent to the terms stated in a proposed contract would not be binding, but acting upon those terms, by sending coal in the quantities and at the price mentioned in if, amounted, to the adoption of the writing previously altered and sent, and to constitute it a valid contract. 

 10. In an arbitration agreement the implied acceptance of the contract has been so held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Muhammad Saghir Bhatti & Sons Vs. Federation of Pakistan. The passage on the point says "that the argument was that after the first arbitrator was appointed, Quarter Master General had no power to make without the permission of the Court, another appointment; but the appellant did not raise this objection at the time the third arbitrator started holding the enquiry. In the circumstances the appellant must be deemed to have agreed to the appointment of Mr. Murshed as the Arbitrator." In view of the authorities set out above, we do not think it worthwhile to refer to other judicial authorities cited from the Bar. 

 12. The dispute centred round the stage when the appellant filed an application dated 7-10-67 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, stating that Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury had declined to act as Umpire, and prayed for the substitution of Mr. Sharafatullah in his place. It was also prayed that the power of Respondent's attorney had ceased and a fresh agreement by the owners themselves may be executed. The record shows that on 14-10-67, the Arbitrator Mr. Z. Abedin Chowdhury had received the memorandum from the Additional Deputy Commissioner appointing him as Arbitrator and on 1-11-67 he issued notices on the parties, the day held by the Courts below to be the date of reference of arbitration. It appears that the Respondent through his attorney, on 27-11-67 made another proposal and, in it was stated that the Appellant's proposal to the appointment of Mr. Sharafatullah as Umpire was not agreed to by him. It was prayed that the appointment of the Umpire might be cancelled keeping Mr. Z. Abedin Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator in the case, as the appointment of umpire was uncalled for, and on that date the Additional Deputy Commissioner made an order by which he amended his earlier order dated 28-9-67 so far it related to the appointment of Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury as umpire. He amended the earlier order of 28-9-67 saying that "there shall be now no umpire for referring the award of the sole arbitrator. The award of sole Arbitrator shall be binding on both the parties." This was done on 27-11-67 and on 28-11-67 the Respondent himself wrote a letter to the Arbitrator, which was received by him on 29-11-67, saying that he would abide by the award which may be made. 

 13. The facts set out above clearly indicate, that the arbitration agreement was modified by deleting the second arbitration or the umpire clause stipulated between the parties earlier. The Respondent by writing a letter has clearly accepted the modification of the arbitration agreement. Indeed, it was his proposal that was given effect to by the Additional Deputy Commissioner. The proposal of the appellant to enter into a fresh arbitration agreement and appointment of Mr. Sharafatullah Chowdhury as umpire was not accepted by the Respondent. It is manifest that the original arbitration agreement was modified and accepted by the Respondent. The only question is whether it was accepted by the Appellant as well. We have earlier set out the authorities which say that the arbitration agreement need not be signed and that acceptance of a proposal can be inferred from the conduct of parties or by performance. In case of Muhammad Sagbir Bhatti, the Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that submission to the reference of the Arbitrator may amount to acceptance. The High Court has clearly found and for which there is ample evidence on record that, the Appellant not only submitted to the jurisdiction of the sole Arbitrator. but participated, though not whole-heartedly, in the arbitration proceeding. He appeared before the Arbitrator from time to time, prayed for time, and on 8-2-68 filed an application along with traced copy of R.S. map and another traced copy of P.S. Map showing there, his measurement of different points as also one sheet of P. S. schedule showing measurement of different P.S. plots. It is true that he did not appear in the final stage of the arbitration proceeding. From these facts, we find that the High Court was perfectly justified in inferring the acceptance by the appellant by his conduct of modification of the arbitration agreement which deleted the umpire clause. We will however observe that the High Court is not clear or correct in saying that the parties gave a go-bye to the Ekrarnama dated 28-9-67 and agreed to be bound by a new agreement in the matter being decided by the sole Arbitrator Mr. Z. A. Chowdhury, on 27-11-67 which reflected the agreement of the parties to the dispute. The learned Judges conclusion is correct but the reasoning is not, and that harmless error has not affected the merit of their decision. We find that the appellant by his participation in the arbitration proceeding, has, by his conduct, accepted the modified arbitration agreement as stated in the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner dated 27-11-67. The subsequent conduct of the appellant also reveals that he did accept the modified agreement by his conduct in fact. He got the first opportunity to challenge the question when the award was filed before the Subordinate Judge and he was called upon to put in his objection. He did raise several grounds of objection but this question was never raised. On the contrary, his objection, which was found by the trial Court barred by, limitation, described Mr. Z. Abedin Chowdhury as the sole arbitrator, and his lengthy grounds traversed on the misconduct of the arbitrator, rather than the want of jurisdiction. His main contention was that the modification of the umpire clause made the entire reference void, as it was not consented to by the Appellant, and that it was a new contract. The trial Court however did not consider whether the appellant by his conduct accepted this modified contract. We have, however, observed that both the Courts below proceeded on a wrong assumption that by modification of the umpire clause, a new arbitration agreement was brought info existence. The application of the appellant and the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner on 27-11-67 clearly says that the order dated 28-9-67 so far it related to the appointment of Mr. Alimullah Chowdhury was being modified. In the face of this clear expression, the Courts below were in error in treating the modification as an error in over looking the fact that this modified substitution of a new agreement. This trial court in arbitration agreement was accepted by the conduct of the appellant. The High Court is correct in inferring so and was perfectly justified in reversing the decision of the trial Court. With somewhat different reasons we accept the decision of the High Court. 

 15. We turn to Mr. Khandker's application to urge some new grounds not covered by the leave order but contained in leave petition. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed filed a written objection praying for its rejection. He in his turn has filed an application praying us to take note of certain facts that developed during the pendency of the proceeding. On hearing the learned Counsel of both sides, we do not think it appropriate to entertain any of the two applications of the rival parties and we reject them. In the result the appeal is dismissed but in the circumstances of the case, we make no order as to costs.
